result:
The answer is most likely 6 (the octahedron), and none of the three proposed answers (50, 7, 8) matches it. I did not fully verify the octahedron's exceptionality, so this rests partly on my recollection of the theorem.

**Solution 2 (7)** cannot be right. No simple 4-regular planar graph on 7 vertices exists, so it cannot be the exceptional graph.

**Solution 1 (50)** is not supported. It relies on a "Möbius strip" claim that has no basis here.

**Solution 3 (8)** claims the square antiprism without proof. I checked the octahedron, which Solution 3 dismissed.

**Octahedron check.**
- A 1-regular conflict graph is a perfect matching on the 12 edges.
- Each single-vertex cut is a 4-edge star. To block all six of these, every vertex needs a matched pair inside its star.
- That uses six pairs covering all 12 edges, so every pair sits at one vertex. This is the same as an orientation with in-degree 2 at every vertex, where the pair at a vertex is its two incoming edges.
- A cut (S, V∖S) is conflict-free exactly when no vertex has both in-neighbours on the opposite side. So a bad matching needs an orientation in which no vertex set S has every vertex with an in-neighbour on its own side.
- Cuts with |S| = 1 or 2 are always blocked. For |S| = 2 with an adjacent pair, a single edge cannot give both vertices an in-neighbour inside S.
- Only splits into two opposite triangular faces could be conflict-free. These need both faces to be directed cycles.
- So it suffices to find an in-degree-2 orientation where no pair of opposite faces is both cyclic. I built part of one by making a face transitive (1→2, 2→3, 1→3), and I expect it extends so that no opposite pair is both cyclic, but I did not complete the check.
- If so, the octahedron has a conflict graph with no conflict-free cut, which makes it the exceptional graph with 6 vertices.

CHOICE: NONE
